newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonian PM sparks fresh crisis as says to quit.
newsitem.headline: Estonian PM sparks fresh crisis as says to quit.

text.p: Estonian Prime Minister Tiit Vaehi said on Wednesday he would resign, sparking a fresh political crisis in the Baltic state.
Leading political parties held emergency talks after Vaehi's announcement, which was prompted by a humiliating no-confidence vote on Monday that he only narrowly won.
Vaehi is leading Estonia's sixth government since the country quit the former Soviet Union in 1991 and said he would quit as soon as a new government was formed.
Vaehi currently leads a minority government, composed of his Coalition Party and a bloc of rural parties.
Vaehi, a veteran politician who came to power in April 1995, has already been through two political crises.
"Under the present balance of political powers, there is no point for me to continue as prime minister," Vaehi said in a statement.

"I have decided to step down as prime minister as soon as political parties have agreed on forming a new government enjoying parliamentary support and have also found a candidate for prime minister," he added.
The Coalition Party said it would choose someone to hold talks with other parties on forming a new government.
"The Coalition Party will meet tonight to decide who will be authorised to conduct talks with other political parties and with what mandate," a Coalition Party spokesman told Reuters.

Vaehi said he was making clear he wanted to resign after a statement on Tuesday, in which he said that he would launch talks to form a more solid government. He said this had been misinterpreted to mean he wanted to hang on to power.
Vaehi first came to power in April 1995 on a wave of public discontent over radical free-market reforms and scandals under a previous right-wing government.
Despite fears he would slow down reforms, Vaehi has pushed ahead with privatisation and helped make Estonia one of the best economic performers of the former Soviet Union.
Vaehi's current government enjoys the firm support of 41 members of the 101-seat parliament and around five or six independent deputies.
He only narrowly survived the no-confidence vote, with 45 MPs backing it and 46 deputies supporting Vaehi.
Some opposition parties said they were willing to work with Vaehi's party in government if Vaehi was not prime minister.

"I personally consider it improbable that we could participate in a coalition led by Prime Minister Tiit Vaehi," Rein Voog, a member of leading opposition party, the Reform Party, told the domestic news agency ETA.
